planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring or fall against a sturdy trellis, arbor, or wall where the self-clinging tendril discs can grip; this selection tolerates colder winters than typical crossvine, so it holds its evergreen foliage further north.

directions: Jekyll was selected on Jekyll Island, Georgia for its combination of glossy evergreen foliage and improved cold tolerance compared to typical crossvine seedlings. Plant against masonry, chain link, or a heavy arbor since the adhesive tendril tips climb without twining and cling tightly once attached. Orange-red, two-inch trumpet flowers with yellow throats open in flushes from mid-spring into early summer and draw hummingbirds heavily. Once established it tolerates drought, part shade, and poor soil, needing only an annual post-bloom trim to keep it in bounds.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring against a sturdy support such as a fence, pergola post, or brick wall; this Texas-origin selection tolerates part shade better than most crossvine cultivars, making it a good fit for a partly shaded pergola.

directions: Selected from a Texas population, Helen Fredel bears unusually large, two-inch flared orange trumpets with a distinct yellow-orange throat that shows off against the semi-evergreen leaves. It climbs by adhesive tendril tips rather than twining, so it needs a solid vertical surface rather than wire it can pull loose. Bloom is heaviest in mid-spring with scattered rebloom into summer, and hummingbirds visit constantly during the main flush. It is otherwise as tough and low-maintenance as the species, tolerating heat, occasional drought, and light shade once its roots are established.

planting.note: Site against a very sturdy arbor, pergola, or fence in spring; this selection is more compact and less rampant by suckering than typical trumpet vine but still needs a support that can bear real weight.

directions: Indian Summer produces the same hummingbird-magnet clusters of orange-red, reddish-throated trumpets as wild trumpet vine but on a noticeably more restrained, better-behaved plant. It blooms on new wood from late spring through summer, so prune hard in late winter to encourage compact growth and heavy flower set the following season. It clings by aerial rootlets to masonry and wood and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Because it still suckers to some degree, keep a mowed or edged perimeter around the planting site to control spread.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall on a fence, mailbox post, or light trellis in moist, well-drained soil; Cedar Lane tolerates part shade well but flowers most heavily with several hours of direct sun.

directions: Introduced by Cedar Lane Farms in Madison, Georgia, this selection is distinguished from other coral honeysuckle cultivars by its narrow, glaucous blue-green foliage and long, slender vermillion-red trumpets with yellow throats. It twines lightly rather than clinging, so give it wire, lattice, or twiggy shrub branches to grasp. Whorled flower clusters open heavily in May and June with sporadic repeat bloom into fall, followed by red berries that songbirds strip quickly. It is a well-behaved, non-invasive native alternative to Japanese honeysuckle and needs only light pruning after the main bloom flush to stay tidy.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant on a heavy-duty arbor, pergola, or pillar in slightly acidic, moist, well-drained soil; unlike Asian wisteria this native selection does not need training onto weak supports it will eventually crush, but the mature vine is still substantial.

directions: Discovered as a wild white-flowered form of American wisteria, Nivea produces dense, fragrant six-to-ten-inch racemes of pure white flowers with pale yellow centers in late spring, occasionally followed by a lighter summer rebloom. It is far less aggressive than Chinese or Japanese wisteria, blooms at a younger age, and does not seed itself into surrounding woodland. It tolerates a bit of part shade with some loss of flower production, so for the fullest bloom give it as much direct sun as the site allows. Prune immediately after flowering to control size and encourage flower buds for the following year.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant on a mailbox trellis, fence, or as a groundcover in fall or spring in well-drained soil; Margarita tolerates significantly colder winters than seed-grown Carolina jessamine, so it is a reliable choice at the cooler edge of the species' range.

directions: Margarita was selected by plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens in Georgia for larger, more fragrant canary-yellow trumpet flowers and notably better cold hardiness than typical Carolina jessamine. It twines readily onto wire, lattice, or shrub branches and can also be left unsupported as a dense evergreen groundcover on a bank. Flowering is heaviest in early spring in full sun but still respectable in part shade, making it useful under high pine canopy. All plant parts are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where livestock or small children graze.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring at a woodland edge, fence line, or open thicket where the sprawling stems can scramble over shrubs or light wire; keep the root zone shaded and mulched while the top growth reaches for sun.

directions: Satincurls is a sprawling, semi-woody native clematis of coastal plain woodlands and calcareous thickets from Virginia to Florida and west into Louisiana, closely related to the more northern virgin's bower but restricted to the warmer, sandier soils of the southeastern coastal plain. Small, fragrant, four-petaled white flowers appear in loose clusters from late summer into fall, followed by the fluffy, silvery seed plumes typical of the genus. It scrambles rather than climbs strongly, so give it shrubs, a low fence, or brush to lean on, and let it ramble at a partly shaded woodland edge rather than forcing it up a bare trellis. It is an easy, low-input native for naturalized Gulf Coast plantings and provides late-season nectar for a range of pollinators.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
